title: Long-horizon autoformalization of a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE
authors: Sirui Lu, Ruixuan Deng, Yanqiao Zhu, Zhengfeng Ji
abstract: Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving and review loops. Agents strengthen verification and review throughout formalization. We completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE. Developing the proof took 63 days; greater parallelism could further reduce this time. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. The formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate errors while preserving the published final error bound under corrected assumptions. This work provides a verified foundation for quantum complexity and demonstrates a route to affordable verification of major research proofs by small teams.
summary: This paper introduces FormalFlow, a novel autoformalization system designed to tackle the immense challenge of verifying complex mathematical theorems over long time horizons. By treating proof construction like software engineering, the authors successfully formalized the quantum soundness of the LIDT, demonstrating a powerful, reproducible route for verifying foundational results in quantum complexity theory.
main_problem: The core challenge is the long-horizon autoformalization of complex mathematical theorems, specifically proving the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test (LIDT), a key component underlying the $	ext{MIP}^* = 	ext{RE}$ result.
main_result: The authors successfully generated a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the LIDT, resulting in a library of over 126,000 lines of code, while correcting several errors in the original published statements.
method: They developed FormalFlow, an autoformalization framework that coordinates AI proving agents using software engineering principles, shared blueprints, and nested planning/review loops to manage complexity and prevent statement drift.
model_or_system: The underlying mathematical model involves the Low-Degree Test (LIDT), which tests the quantum soundness of a polynomial $g$ of low individual degree, typically involving shared quantum entanglement between two provers (Alice and Bob).
key_observables: The process tracks proof gaps, open obligations, compiler diagnostics (sorry count), and the successful formalization of the quantum soundness theorem.
important_parameters: The proof was completed over 63 days of agent work, and the final code base size is 126,367 lines of Lean code.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that by rigorously applying software engineering principles to mathematical proof construction, the verification of major theorems can become an affordable, automated process.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the nested scales of work (planning, review, work session) involving humans and AI agents. Figure 2 tracks progress metrics like blueprint completion and compiler diagnostics over time. Figure 3 details the formal proof architecture for the LIDT.
paper_structure: The paper details the FormalFlow framework, its operational scales (macro, meso, micro), the process of using a shared blueprint to map informal claims to formal Lean declarations, and the step-by-step process of auditing and repairing the complex LIDT proof.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, scalable methodology for verifying foundational theorems in quantum complexity theory, which underpins many quantum information protocols.
